title: Short Stuff: All About Egg Colors
summary: Short Stuff episode on why chicken eggs come in different colors. Josh and Chuck open with a story about Chuck's camp trip and his friend Justin, who raises chickens and supplied eggs of several colors. They explain that white eggs are not bleached and that shell color is not a nutritional difference; white eggs come from Leghorn hens, while breeds like Plymouth Rock, Orpington, and Rhode Island Red lay brown eggs, and the Americauna lays blue-tinted eggs. Justin Fowler, a University of Georgia poultry scientist, says earlobe color can hint at egg color. The hosts then trace the egg through the oviduct: the shell forms in the shell gland, starting white from calcium carbonate, and pigment is deposited afterward. Two pigments, biliverdin (blue-green) and protoporphyrin (reddish-brown), produce the colors; Robin's eggs and common murre eggs are also mentioned. They discuss pasture-raised versus cage-free and free-range eggs, noting that "pasture raised" is not regulated in the US and that certifications like Certified Humane exist. Last, they cover washing eggs: commercial eggs are washed in the US, Japan, and Australia, which removes the protective bloom and requires refrigeration, while unwashed local eggs can be kept unrefrigerated until washed.

segments.title: Opening banter and egg-price setup
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode on chicken egg colors and joke about expensive eggs.

segments.title: Chuck's camp trip and Justin's eggs
segments.summary: Chuck describes his annual camp trip, where his friend Justin, who raises chickens, brought eggs of different colors, prompting the question of why they differ.

segments.title: Brown vs white eggs and breeds
segments.summary: The hosts say white eggs are not bleached and that brown and white eggs have the same nutrition. White eggs come from Leghorn hens, while Plymouth Rock and Orpington hens lay brown eggs and Americauna hens lay blue-tinted eggs.

segments.title: Earlobes and egg color genetics
segments.summary: Justin Fowler, a University of Georgia poultry scientist, explains that genetics determine egg color and that earlobe color can indicate whether a hen lays tinted or white eggs. The hosts joke about chicken earlobes.

segments.title: Trip through the oviduct and shell formation
segments.summary: The hosts describe the egg's path through the oviduct. The shell forms in the shell gland from white calcium carbonate, and some breeds then deposit pigment on it.

segments.title: Pigments behind egg colors
segments.summary: Two pigments, biliverdin (blue-green) and protoporphyrin (reddish-brown), produce the range of egg colors. Robin's eggs and common murre eggs are mentioned as similar blue eggs.

segments.title: Egg dyeing versus natural color
segments.summary: The hosts joke about Easter egg dyeing compared with the natural patterns chickens can produce.

segments.title: Pasture raised, cage free, and free range eggs
segments.summary: Chuck says pasture-raised eggs may have slightly more omega-3 and vitamins, and that free range often just means a barn door is open. Josh notes that 'pasture raised' is not regulated in the US and points to certifications such as Certified Humane.

segments.title: Buying local eggs
segments.summary: Chuck recommends sourcing eggs locally, such as from farmers markets or friends, which can be cheaper than grocery store eggs during high prices.

segments.title: Washing eggs and the bloom
segments.summary: Josh explains that commercial eggs are washed in the US, Japan, and Australia, which removes the protective waxy coating (bloom) and requires refrigeration. Unwashed local eggs can stay unrefrigerated until washed. Washing can leave bacteria like salmonella on the egg, so the advice is to keep local eggs unwashed until use.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up the episode and the show credits.
